issues.legal_issue: The first hearing of a civil suit ordinarily occurs after the issues have been framed, when the court applies its mind to the parties’ contentions or takes evidence.
material_facts: The defendant appeared on the date fixed for the return of summons, filed a written statement, and gave a statement in court.
The statement was recorded before issues had been framed, and the suit was later disposed of on the basis of the parties’ statements.
issues.conclusion: The date fixed for the return of summons was not the first hearing of the suit, and the statement recorded then was taken before the first hearing in the procedural sense.
issues.legal_principle: On a conjoint reading of Order X Rule 1, Order XIV Rule 1(5), and Order XV Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure, the first hearing ordinarily occurs after issues are framed, when the court applies its mind to the pleadings and documents or evidence is taken. The Court relied on Ved Prakash Wadhwa v. Vishwa Mohan, AIR 1982 SC 816; Sham Lal v. Atma Nand Jain Sabha, AIR 1987 SC 197; Siraj Ahmad Siddiqui v. Shri Prem Nath Kapoor, AIR 1993 SC 2525; and M/s Mangat Singh Trilochan Singh v. Satpal, AIR 2003 SC 4300.

predicates.civil_suit: The proceeding is a civil suit.
predicates.statement_taken_on_summons_return_date: The court records a party’s statement on the date fixed for the return of summons.
predicates.issues_not_yet_framed: The court has not yet framed the issues in the suit.

issues.definition: When a statement in a civil suit is recorded on the summons return date before issues have been framed, that occasion is not the first hearing.

issues.legal_issue: A breach of an undertaking incorporated into a final injunction decree must be pursued through execution rather than through proceedings for breach of an interim injunction or as a means of enforcing the decree through contempt.
material_facts: The civil court disposed of the suit by a final decree based on the defendant’s undertaking not to dispossess the plaintiff.
No interim injunction had been granted during the suit.
After the decree, the plaintiff sought action for breach of the undertaking under a procedure for breach of an interim injunction and through contempt proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The post-decree application under Order XXXIX Rule 2A CPC was not maintainable; the remedy for breach of the decree was execution under Order XXI Rule 32 CPC, and contempt jurisdiction could not be used as a mode of executing the decree.
issues.legal_principle: Order XXXIX Rule 2A CPC applies to disobedience of an injunction or order made under Order XXXIX Rules 1 and 2 during the pendency of a suit; once the suit is decreed, the interim order merges into the final order. Breach of an injunction decree, including an undertaking that has become part of the decree, is to be addressed through execution under Order XXI Rule 32 CPC. The Court relied on Food Corporation of India v. Sukha Deo Prasad, AIR 2009 SC 2330, and Hungerford Investment Trust Ltd. v. Haridas Mundhra, AIR 1972 SC 1826, among other authorities.

predicates.post_decree_breach_proceeding: A party seeks sanctions for breach after the suit has ended in a final decree.
predicates.final_injunction_decree: The final decree directs a party to refrain from an act or to perform an act.
predicates.undertaking_incorporated_into_decree: A party’s undertaking to the court forms part of the final decree.

issues.definition: When a party seeks sanctions for breaching an undertaking incorporated into a final injunction decree after the suit has ended, the breach must be pursued through execution.

issues.legal_issue: A breach of an undertaking or decree in a civil dispute concerning private rights does not, without sufficient public interest or obstruction of the administration of justice, constitute criminal contempt.
material_facts: The alleged breach concerned an undertaking made in a civil suit between private parties and incorporated into the decree disposing of that suit.
The complainant’s grievance was the alleged breach of the decree, for which the civil procedure provided an enforcement remedy.
The trial court referred the matter for criminal contempt, and the High Court convicted the defendant based in part on inconsistent pleas in his later response.
issues.conclusion: The alleged breach could at most amount to civil contempt; it did not warrant criminal contempt proceedings on these facts.
issues.legal_principle: Section 2(b) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 includes the wilful breach of an undertaking given to a court within civil contempt. The distinction is that civil contempt enforces an order for the benefit of one party against another, whereas criminal contempt protects the authority of the court and the administration of justice. The Court relied on Samee Khan v. Bindu Khan, AIR 1998 SC 2765, and on Niaz Mohammad v. State of Haryana, (1994) 6 SCC 332; Bank of Baroda v. Sadruddin Hasan Daya, AIR 2004 SC 942; and Rama Narang v. Ramesh Narang, AIR 2006 SC 1883.

rule.if: private_civil_dispute and breach_of_private_party_obligation and adequate_civil_enforcement_remedy and not substantial_public_obstruction

predicates.private_civil_dispute: The alleged breach arises in a civil dispute concerning the rights of private parties.
predicates.breach_of_private_party_obligation: The alleged conduct is a breach of an undertaking or decree made for the benefit of another party to the dispute.
predicates.adequate_civil_enforcement_remedy: A civil procedure is available to enforce the undertaking or decree.
predicates.substantial_public_obstruction: The alleged conduct substantially obstructs the administration of justice or affects public interest beyond the private dispute.

issues.definition: A breach of an obligation owed to a private party in a civil dispute, where a civil enforcement remedy exists and substantial public obstruction is absent, is not criminal contempt.

issues.legal_issue: Punishment for contempt requires clear proof of intentional obstruction of the administration of justice and cannot rest on surmise or conjecture.
material_facts: The contempt conviction arose from proceedings that were not maintainable as a means of enforcing the final decree.
The High Court relied in part on inconsistent pleas in the defendant’s response to the application.
The alleged contemnor faced imprisonment, and the Supreme Court found the proceedings had been conducted without the required procedure.
issues.conclusion: The contempt conviction could not stand where the proceedings were legally unavailable and the case did not establish a clear basis for criminal contempt through the required standard of proof.
issues.legal_principle: Contempt proceedings are quasi-criminal, so the alleged contemnor is entitled to the safeguards of criminal jurisprudence, including the benefit of doubt. There must be a clear case of intentional obstruction of the administration of justice, not one based on surmise or conjecture. The Court relied on Debabrata Bandopadhyay v. State of West Bengal, AIR 1969 SC 189.

predicates.contempt_proceeding: The court is considering whether to punish a person for contempt.
predicates.evidence_of_intentional_obstruction_is_u: The evidence does not clearly establish intentional obstruction of the administration of justice.

issues.definition: A person facing contempt punishment cannot be punished when the proceeding is for contempt and the evidence does not clearly establish intentional obstruction of the administration of justice.
